overview.text: Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) is a virus that weakens the immune system by infecting CD4 T cells, white blood cells that help defend the body against infections. Its replication strategy is distinctive: after entering a CD4 cell, HIV uses reverse transcriptase to convert its RNA into DNA, then integrates viral DNA into the cell’s DNA so the cell can help make new viruses. Without treatment, loss of CD4 cells can leave the body vulnerable to serious infections and some cancers. This advanced stage of HIV infection is called acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS), not a separate virus. Antiretroviral therapy (ART) can suppress HIV and protect health, but it does not eliminate the virus.

key_facts.text: HIV stands for human immunodeficiency virus; AIDS stands for acquired immunodeficiency syndrome.
HIV targets CD4 T cells, immune-system white blood cells that help protect the body from infection.
Reverse transcriptase converts HIV’s RNA into DNA; another enzyme, integrase, helps insert that DNA into a CD4 cell’s DNA.
AIDS is a late stage of HIV infection, not a separate virus; it occurs when the immune system is badly damaged.
ART can control HIV and lower its amount in the blood, but it is not a cure and the virus remains in the body.
